A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cognitive-model study despite the changed title and organization. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised, added, and removed content.

before.justification: V1 reports original LLM response analyses, inferred utility parameters, and training-checkpoint experiments with Qwen and Llama under DPO and PPO (Figures 2–3 and Appendix C).

after.justification: V3 retains original LLM experiments and adds communicative-goal manipulations and held-out predictive results (Figures 3–6 and Appendices C–D). The human reference results remain attributed to Yoon et al.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same recursive RSA cognitive model, three utility components, literal-semantics estimation, and Stan inference procedure. The SFT followed by DPO or PPO training procedure is retained. New goal prompts manipulate the evaluated LLMs rather than alter the cognitive inference method.

E1.justification: V3 extends the retained polite-feedback vignettes to conditions explicitly requiring informative feedback, social comfort, or both. This adds task requirements within the existing domain; the original vignettes, literal-semantics task, three framings, UltraFeedback, and HH-RLHF coverage remain.

E2.justification: V3 adds an S2 baseline with randomly sampled parameters for predictive validation (Appendix C.2, Figure 6). V1's comparison with a simplified S1 model disappears (Appendix C.3, Figure 16). The human reference and membership of the main LLM evaluation suites are retained.

E3.justification: V3 introduces an 80/20 fitting/test split and held-out posterior predictive evaluation using MSE. The stated per-state count used for cognitive-model fitting changes from 130 to 104 (v1 Appendix B.2; v3 Appendix C.2). Goal instructions also become an experimental factor crossed with existing conditions. These substantially expand the evaluation design; LLM training budgets and Table 2 hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 adds controlled analyses of how communicative goals shift inferred utilities and interact with reasoning, including the proposed sycophancy signature (Sections 5.2.1–5.2.2). It also adds held-out predictive validation while removing v1's S1 simplification check. This substantially changes the evidence testing sensitivity and validity of the inferred parameters.

E5.justification: V3 adds significance reporting for the held-out MSE comparison. Four inference chains, 2,000 warm-up iterations, 2,000 samples per chain, and 95% highest-density intervals are retained. V1 Figure 2 displays uncertainty separately by reasoning level; v3 Figure 3 omits those intervals, while Figure 4 reports uncertainty pooled across reasoning levels and framings.

E6.justification: V3 adds goal-conditioned utility findings and held-out MSE results of 0.03 for inferred versus 0.06 for random parameters (z = -12.49, p < 0.001), and removes the S1 results. Retained estimates and appendix response distributions also change: the low/medium reasoning coefficients for phi change from 0.21/0.19 to 0.228/0.211. These accompany revised fitting settings and do not establish same-setting performance gains. The open-source prose also switches the stronger social-utility dataset-effect description from PPO to DPO.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4, recursive speaker/listener definitions, utility functions, the identity social-value mapping, and equal utterance-cost assumption are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears. The added random-parameter distributions specify a validation baseline.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions add the claim that explicit goal prompts predictably shift utility patterns and qualify the reasoning-model finding as describing default behavior. The central cognitive-interpretation contribution and claims about early training shifts and persistent base-model effects remain.

C2.justification: V1 reports no strong examples of its hypothesized sycophancy signature and suggests it may not be a widespread safety concern. V3 interprets patterns induced by social-goal prompts as that signature and hypothesizes selective reinforcement of prompted attributes through reasoning (Section 5.2.2). It also discusses greater stability of informational utility and newly reports difficulties generating open-ended utterance alternatives and using their continuation probabilities.

D1.justification: V3 supplies exact communicative-goal prompts and random-baseline sampling distributions (Appendices B.5 and C.2). It omits v1's explicit study code/data repository link and statement that answer-option order was randomized. Model identifiers, training hyperparameters, hardware, and training-time disclosures remain available.

R1.justification: V3 adds references including Bonawitz et al., Hu and Levy, Itzhak et al., and Qiu et al., while dropping Cui et al.'s UltraFeedback reference and several vendor-documentation references. The central positioning relative to RSA, inverse RL, and Liu et al. remains. Most background material is relocated to Appendix A.

P1.justification: V3 retitles the paper, rewrites and condenses substantial introductory, evaluation-suite, and discussion prose, and moves the full Background section into the appendix. Existing response-processing and inference details are consolidated there, while closed-source results are reorganized around default behavior, communicative goals, and sycophancy.

P2.justification: V3 adds an introductory conceptual illustration, redraws the paradigm overview, and replaces the original closed-source bar-chart presentation with reasoning-budget curves and a goal-comparison chart. It adds the predictive-check figure, removes the S1 figure, and moves Table 1 into the appendix. The open-source plot is recolored, although its caption retains the old purple/magenta descriptions.

improvement.justification: V3 strengthens empirical support by comparing human and LLM behavior under analogous goal instructions and checking predictions on held-out data (Figures 4 and 6), extending v1's default-behavior analyses. These gains are tempered by removal of the S1 diagnostic and explicit code/data link. The new sycophancy interpretation also remains based on prompted utility patterns, with validation on explicitly sycophantic models still proposed as future work.
